# On Tajikarao: a letter to a colleague

*A letter to a colleague, 31 July 2026 — on the name Tajikarao, and on the forms that keep failing it.*

Your note said, roughly: surely the marks are a nicety. Permit me to use Tajikarao to show they are not.

First, the attestation. The name is attested as **手力男神**, as Kojiki, Ama-no-Iwato narrative (Kamitsumaki) and Nihon Shoki, Age of the Gods, Scroll I record. On the evidence, it means "Strong hand man". The canonical transliteration is **Tajikarao**.

Say it aloud as the sources heard it: 'TAH-jee-kah-rah-oh' — the 'j' is soft, and the 'r' is a light tap. The marks are what carry that sound to a reader who has never heard it spoken.

On the plain form — and I want to be precise, because you pushed on this. The plain form *tajikarao* differs from the canonical *Tajikarao* only by convention of display — case, not content. It is *acceptable everywhere*: in legacy systems, in plain-text citation, in the DNS itself. What is not acceptable is what follows in the register: respellings that change the letters, not just their case.

One more thing, because it always surprises: the name did not stay home. Tajikarao resists syncretism precisely because his role is so pure: he is the strong arm inside a theology of coordinated function.  In the Ama-no-Iwato assembly every kami performs one office — Uzume the dance, Futotama the rope, Koyane the words, Tajikarao the hand — a picture of the kami as functionaries in a cosmic administration that Shinto reflection has read ever since as a model of communal harmony (wa).

And it never stopped working. Tajikarao's living monument is Togakushi.  The shrine complex above Nagano, approached by an avenue of centuries-old cedars, draws pilgrims and hikers to the Oku-sha and worshippers seeking strength and favorable outcomes to its Middle Shrine; the mountains acquired a second, separate fame in the medieval period as the legendary home of the Togakure-ryū ninja tradition — the 'hidden door' serving concealment as well as revelation.

## The Convention's Own History

Every tradition in this register has its own scholarly transliteration standard, built by its own specialists over decades or centuries, and the register follows each on its own terms: Hepburn with macrons — ō and ū marked, never collapsed to o/u or rewritten ou. The principle that unifies them is the one the whole project stands on: a name is evidence, and evidence is not negotiable — not for keyboards, not for convenience, not for anyone.

## The Address, Without an Encoding Detour

The canonical form **Tajikarao** already uses ordinary Latin letters, so the address bar needs no special encoding narrative. The digital temple can preserve the spelling exactly as the scholarly record presents it. That is the practical point here: consistency between the source, the citation, and the public address.

This does not make every romanization equally valid. A wrong letter remains wrong even when it is easy to type. Canonical status still depends on the attested convention, never on convenience or registrar inventory.

Write back when you have checked the sources; they are better company than I am.

*— The Register*

## The Verdict

**Tajikarao** is the canonical form: attested, checkable, and enforced across the temple, the lexicon, the cards, the APIs, and this register. The plain form *tajikarao* shares that standing — the two are the same name in every system. The false forms above are documented so that no reader has to take the temple's word on faith — the violations are stated, the sources are named, and the register stands open to challenge on every line.

The temple of **Tajikarao** stands at [/tajikarao/](/tajikarao/).

The docket for this ruling: no false forms on the docket; no contested forms attested; the attestation rests on 5 cited sources — Kojiki, Ama-no-Iwato narrative (Kamitsumaki), Nihon Shoki, Age of the Gods, Scroll I, Philippi, Kojiki (Princeton, 1968).
